note: Gold-standard scripts per niche. 2 examples each. Injected into the system prompt as few-shot demonstrations — the model mimics these more than any instruction, so they define the voice: open on the VIEWER or a sharp take, use the famous name as PROOF mid-script (never as the subject of a biography), present tense and second person, a loop line that echoes the hook, and an ending that earns a comment instead of begging for a follow. 85-115 words (34-46s at ~150wpm).

finance.seed_content: The stock market is a device for transferring money from the impatient to the patient.
finance.script:
You checked your portfolio four times today.
That's the problem. Not your salary, not your stock picks. Your hands.
Buffett has held Coca-Cola since 1988 and never sold a single share.
One billion dollars turned into twenty-five billion while he did nothing.
He didn't pick better than you. He refused to move.
The average investor makes eight trades a year and bleeds three percent doing it.
Every one of those trades felt smart in the moment. That's the trap.
The richest investor alive built his fortune sitting still.
You are not under-informed. You are over-active.
So you don't have a strategy problem. You have a patience problem.
How many times did you check today?

finance.seed_content: Do not look for the needle in the haystack. Just buy the haystack.
finance.script:
You think the market is the risky part. It isn't. You are.
The S&P 500 has never lost money over any twenty-year stretch in history.
Not in 2008. Not the Great Depression. Not COVID.
Every single time, it came back higher.
Yet the average investor underperforms that exact index by three percent a year.
Not from bad stocks. From selling during the crashes.
Jack Bogle saw this in 1974 and built Vanguard on one idea.
Stop trying to beat the market. Own all of it.
The index never fails people. People fail the index.
So the risk was never the market. The risk is you.
Which crash are you going to sell into next?

motivation.seed_content: We suffer more in imagination than in reality.
motivation.script:
The thing you're dreading right now has already beaten you.
Seneca said it two thousand years ago: we suffer more in imagination than in reality.
That conversation you've put off for a week.
The call you keep dragging to next Monday.
You've been living inside the worst version of it for days.
Then you finally do it, and it takes five minutes.
And you sit there wondering what you were so afraid of.
The dread always costs more than the thing. Every single time.
You're not avoiding the task. You're feeding the fear.
So what are you rehearsing right now instead of just doing?
Name the thing. Then go do it today.

motivation.seed_content: The most important conversations you will ever have are the ones you will have with yourself.
motivation.script:
Your body quit at forty percent. You called it your limit.
Goggins ran a hundred miles on two broken feet.
Not because he's built different. Because he learned to argue with the voice that says stop.
He says your mind throttles you at forty percent of what you have left.
The rest is a negotiation. Not with your legs — with your own head.
Most people take the first exit their mind offers and obey it instantly.
They feel the urge to stop and call it a wall.
You have never actually hit your ceiling.
You only believed the voice that said this is it.
So that wasn't your limit. That was your first offer.
What are you negotiating with right now?

mindset.seed_content: Everything that irritates us about others can lead us to an understanding of ourselves.
mindset.script:
The person who irritates you most is showing you yourself.
Carl Jung spent decades on why smart people keep repeating the same mistakes.
His answer was the shadow — the part of you that you refuse to look at.
The trait you cannot stand in someone else?
Usually the one you have buried in yourself.
Furious at arrogance — check the ambition you won't admit to.
Disgusted by weakness — check what you're scared to feel.
Jung called it projection. Your loudest judgments are confessions in disguise.
Every strong reaction you have to a person is a map to your blind spot.
So who is it — who has been living rent-free in your head?
Which person were you thinking about just now?

mindset.seed_content: Between stimulus and response there is a space. In that space is our power to choose.
mindset.script:
There's a half-second gap you skip every single day. It's costing you your character.
Viktor Frankl survived three concentration camps.
He watched some people break and others find meaning in the exact same hell.
The difference wasn't strength. Wasn't luck. Wasn't background.
It was the pause between what happened and how they answered.
Frankl called that pause freedom.
Not freedom from your circumstances. Freedom inside your response.
Most people never use it. Stimulus, reaction, no gap.
Then they call that reaction their personality.
So the gap you keep skipping is the only freedom you actually own.
Where are you skipping the pause today?

business.script:
Your competitor's fat profit margin is a map showing you exactly where to attack.
Bezos built Amazon's first strategy on one line: your margin is my opportunity.
Barnes and Noble made forty percent on every book in 1995.
Amazon sold at cost and ate losses for three straight years.
By year four, the bookstore giant could not fight back.
They didn't lose to better books. They lost to their own comfortable margins.
Every fat-margin business is screaming where the opening is.
Thin margins, huge volume, a timeline nobody else will stomach.
That is how you make a giant obsolete without ever being smarter than them.
So whose fat margin are you about to turn into your opening?
What fat-margin market are you about to attack?

You've been building for six months without talking to one user. That's why it will flop.
Paul Graham has funded companies now worth over a trillion dollars combined.
He runs one test on every founder in the first ten minutes.
Not the idea. Not the market. Not the resume.
One question: do you talk to your users every week?
Most founders build in a room for months, then wonder why nobody shows up.
You cannot guess what people want from inside your own head.
Dropbox, Airbnb, Stripe — every one started by talking to ten people.
The product was never the work. The conversation is the work.
So when did you last talk to the person you're building for?
When did you last talk to a real customer?

personal_development.seed_content: You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems.
personal_development.script:
Stop setting goals. They are the reason you keep failing.
James Clear spent three years on why people cannot build habits.
The finding that changed everything: you don't rise to your goals, you fall to your systems.
A goal to run a marathon won't get you up on a cold Tuesday.
Running shoes set by the door the night before will.
It was never about motivation.
It's about how many decisions stand between you and starting.
Kill the decision, and the habit runs itself.
Ten million people bought his book for that single idea.
So you don't need a bigger goal. You need a smaller decision.
What's the one decision you can kill tomorrow?

personal_development.seed_content: Specific knowledge is found by pursuing your genuine curiosity, not whatever is hot right now.
personal_development.script:
You're chasing what's hot. That's exactly why you'll stay average.
Naval Ravikant built two companies, invested early in Uber and Twitter, retired at forty.
He repeats one thing: don't optimize for what's hot, optimize for what you can't stop thinking about.
He calls it specific knowledge.
The expertise that feels like play to you and looks like work to everyone else.
That gap is an edge nobody can grind their way into copying.
You can fake discipline. You cannot fake genuine obsession.
The people who chased trends are doing fine.
The people who chased an obsession built the companies the trend-chasers wish they had started.
So what do you keep circling back to that you've been calling a distraction?
Which one are you starting with — tell me.
